html:
Compulsory Social Studies in the SEE is a 75-mark, three-hour paper. Its very short questions, worth one mark each, are the objective part: a fact, a date, a name, a place.

They are the quickest marks in the paper and the ones lost most often through careless recall.

This chapter gives practice items for all ten units of the Grade 10 Social Studies book, with an answer key and a one-line reason for every item.

About the labels in this chapter

Every item here is an original practice item written to the pattern of the SEE and to the facts of the Social Studies book chapters in this series. None is claimed to be a question from a particular year's paper.

A year printed beside a question is usually a guess, and a wrong label teaches you to trust the wrong thing.

14.1 Where objective items sit in the paper

The Curriculum Development Centre (CDC) grid for Grade 10 Social Studies, as published for the 2080 curriculum, is a 75-mark paper of 24 questions: 11 very short answer questions of 1 mark, 9 short answer questions of 4 marks and 4 long answer questions of 7 marks.

This chapter covers all 11 one-mark very short answer items unit by unit.

Group Questions Marks each Total Style
A. Very short 11 1 11 one fact, one word, a date or a name
B. Short 9 4 36 give reasons, define and explain
C. Long 4 7 28 explain, describe, analyse

The unit hours below are those reported for the Grade 10 curriculum and are a good guide to how the 11 one-mark items are spread: almost every unit supplies one.

Unit Hours (reported) One-mark items to expect
1. Our Society and We 8 1
2. Development and Foundations of Development 10 1
3. Our Social Values and Beliefs 14 1 to 2
4. Social Problems and Solutions 12 1
5. Civic Consciousness 18 1 to 2
6. Our Earth 18 1 to 2
7. Our Past 14 1 to 2
8. Economic Activities 15 1
9. International Relations 11 1
10. Population and Its Management 8 1

How to use the bank

Answer ten items of one unit in five minutes without notes, then check the key. For each miss, find the sentence in the book chapter and write the fact on a card. Numbers, dates and names are what these items test, so the cards should carry numbers, dates and names.

Chapter summary

  • Group A of the paper is 11 one-mark items; the CDC grid then has 9 short (4-mark) and 4 long (7-mark) answers, so Group A is about 15% of the paper.
  • Nepal's key numbers: population 29,164,578 (2021); 142 caste/ethnic groups; 124 languages; 7 provinces; 753 local levels; HoR 275 (165 + 110); NA 59.
  • Key dates: 7 Falgun 2007 (Democracy Day), 1 Poush 2017 (royal coup), 7 Falgun – 26 Chaitra 2046 (Jana Andolan I), 21 Nov 2006 (Peace Accord), 28 May 2008 (republic), 20 Sept 2015 (Constitution), 3 Ashwin 2072.
  • International: Nepal joined the UN in 1955, NAM in 1961, SAARC in 1985, BIMSTEC in 1997, WTO in 2004; the UN has 193 members and 6 organs.
  • Population: growth rate 0.92%, peak 2.62% in 1981, density 198, sex ratio 95.59, literacy 76.2%.
  • Economy: hydropower potential about 83,000 MW, installed about 3,500 MW; VAT 13%; fiscal year begins 1 Shrawan.
  • Earth: temperature falls 6.5 °C per 1,000 m; Kilimanjaro 5,895 m, Aconcagua about 6,960 m, Denali 6,190 m.

Practice questions

Group A: Very short answer (1 mark each)

  1. In how many provinces is Nepal divided? [1]a5b7c9d14
  2. Which organ of the UN sits in The Hague? [1]athe General Assemblybthe Security Councilcthe International Court of Justicedthe Secretariat
  3. On which date is Constitution Day observed? [1]a15 Jesthab3 Ashwinc7 Falgund27 Poush
  4. What does the growth rate of population measure? [1]
Answers to Group A

1. (b) — seven provinces.

2. (c) — ICJ.

3. (b) — 3 Ashwin.

4. The yearly change in population as a percentage of the base population, found as (CBR − CDR) ÷ 10 when migration is ignored.

Group B: Short answer (4 marks each)

  1. Differentiate between weather and climate. [4]
  2. State four causes of human trafficking. [4]
Answers to Group B

1. Weather is the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere in a place; climate is the long-term (30-year) average. Weather changes hour by hour, climate changes slowly; weather is studied in forecasts, climate in climate records.

2. Poverty; illiteracy and lack of awareness; fake job and marriage offers; open borders and weak control.
